summary: Defines the offer/answer model, in which one party describes a desired multimedia session using SDP and the other replies with its own description to agree on a shared view. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: One person proposes, such as video this way and audio that way, and the other says what they can do. They end up agreeing.

questions: how do sip endpoints negotiate media
what is the sdp offer answer model
how to put a call on hold with sdp
subtitle: How two endpoints trade SDP descriptions so both end up agreeing on the same call.

tldr.problem: SDP could describe a session, but for a two-party unicast session a complete view needs information from both sides: two addresses instead of one, and a set of codecs both can use.
tldr.mechanism: One side sends an offer, an SDP message listing streams, codecs, addresses and ports. The other replies with an answer that has a matching media line for every stream in the offer and accepts or rejects each one.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3264 is the mandatory baseline mechanism for SIP. It has since been updated by RFC 6157, RFC 8843 and RFC 9143.

facts.label: RTCP port
facts.value: One higher than the RTP port, by default

today: RFC 3264 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2543 and has been updated by RFC 6157, RFC 8843 and RFC 9143. Read those updates together with this RFC.

sections.title: Why Unicast Sessions Need a Model
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) was first conceived to describe multicast sessions. A multicast session has one global view that every participant shares. A unicast session has two participants, so a complete view needs information from both, and the two must agree on parameters.

The RFC gives two examples. A multicast stream needs one multicast address, but a unicast stream needs two addresses, one for each participant. A multicast session says which codecs are used, but for unicast the codec set has to be found by overlapping what each side supports.

RFC 3264 fills this gap with a simple offer/answer model. How offers and answers are carried is out of scope: the RFC says it is the mandatory baseline mechanism used by SIP.
sections.eli5: A plan for two people needs both people to say something. One has to say where they are standing and what they can do, and so does the other.

sections.title: Protocol Operation and Glare
sections.content:
The model assumes a higher layer protocol, such as SIP, that can carry SDP between the two agents and keeps context so the exchanges are tied together. An offerer sends an offer. The answerer MAY answer or MAY reject it, and how rejection works depends on the higher layer protocol.

The exchange is atomic. If the answer is rejected, the session goes back to the state before the offer, which may mean no session at all.

Either agent MAY send a new offer at any time to update the session. It MUST NOT do so while it holds an unanswered offer from the peer, or while its own earlier offer is still waiting for an answer. If an offer arrives after you sent one but before you got an answer, that is called glare, and the higher layer protocol has to resolve it.
sections.eli5: You take turns. You may not make a new suggestion while the other person is still waiting for your answer, or while you are still waiting for theirs.

sections.title: Making the Offer
sections.content:
An offer MUST be a valid SDP message, with one relaxation: it MAY omit both the e and p lines. It MUST contain exactly one session description. For unicast, the s= line SHOULD be a single space or a dash, and the t= line SHOULD be 0 0 when streams are created and destroyed by outside signaling such as SIP. An offer can contain zero media streams, which means the streams will be added later.

Each stream carries a direction. a=sendonly and a=recvonly mean what they say, a=inactive means neither sending nor receiving for now, and a=sendrecv is the default. For receiving directions, the address and port say where the offerer wants to receive media. For RTP, RTCP goes to the port one higher unless stated otherwise. A port of zero means the stream is not wanted.

The format list on the m= line MUST be in order of preference, with the first format preferred. Several formats mean the offerer can use any of them, so the answerer MAY switch among them mid-session without a new offer. For RTP streams, media descriptions SHOULD include a=rtpmap lines mapping payload types to encodings.

Several streams of different types mean they are wanted at the same time, such as audio and video. Several streams of the same type are also allowed, and the RFC gives a pre-paid calling card example with one stream to the gateway and one to a tone-detecting application.
sections.eli5: The first person says which kinds of toys they want to play with, lists them from favorite to least favorite, and tells the other person which mailbox to put things in.

sections.title: Writing the Answer
sections.content:
The answer MUST have exactly the same number of m= lines as the offer, in the same order, which is how streams are matched up. The t= line MUST equal the offer's, because the session time cannot be negotiated. If the answer differs from the offer in any way, its origin line MUST be different, since a different entity wrote it.

To reject a stream, the answerer sets its port to zero. If no media format is shared for a stream, the answerer MUST reject it. If no format is shared for any stream, the whole offered session is rejected. A unicast stream in the offer gets a unicast address in the answer.

Directions must fit together. A sendonly offer gets recvonly or inactive. A recvonly offer gets sendonly or inactive. A sendrecv offer may get any of the four. An inactive offer MUST get inactive.

The answer lists the formats it can use, in its own preference order, and it is RECOMMENDED to keep the offer's relative order. The offerer MUST then send using a format from the answer, and SHOULD use the first one. For multicast streams the answer is much more constrained: address, port and direction MUST equal the offer, and the format set MUST be equal to or a subset of the offer's.
sections.eli5: The second person answers each question in the same order. If they cannot do one thing, they say 'no thanks' to that one and still answer all the others.

sections.title: Changing a Session Later
sections.content:
Changing a session uses the exact same offer/answer procedure. A new offer repeats the previous SDP with the version in the o= line incremented by one. The new SDP MUST keep a matching media stream for every one in the previous SDP, so the number of m= lines never decreases. Deleted streams stay in place with port zero, and a new stream can reuse that slot.

Changing a port, address or transport follows one pattern: the sender of the change MUST be ready to receive on both old and new until media arrives on the new one. The set of media formats can also change, but for RTP the mapping from a dynamic payload type number to a codec MUST NOT change for the duration of the session. The RFC lists three ways to know when an old format is gone: change ports, use a new set of dynamic payload types, or use a timer, where one minute would typically be more than sufficient.

To put a stream on hold, mark a sendrecv stream sendonly, or a recvonly stream inactive. RFC 2543 used the connection address 0.0.0.0 for hold, which is no longer recommended because it blocks RTCP, fails with IPv6 and breaks connection oriented media.

The RFC also describes using SDP to report capabilities. Such an SDP uses port zero on every media line, so that it cannot accidentally start a stream if read as an offer or answer.
sections.eli5: If you want to change the game halfway, you make a new suggestion and the other person answers it again. While you switch, you keep both old and new mailboxes open so nothing gets lost.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
In the basic exchange, Alice offers one audio stream (payload type 0, PCMU) and two video streams, one with H.261 (payload type 31) and one with MPEG (payload type 32). Bob answers with the audio stream, sets the first video stream's port to 0 to refuse it, and accepts the second. Later Bob changes his audio port from 49920 to 65422 and adds a receive-only audio stream for telephone events, and Alice accepts that as a send-only stream.

The second example is for phones whose signal processor can support several codecs but cannot switch once one is chosen. Alice offers three codecs in an inactive stream, Bob answers with two, and Alice sends an updated offer with a single codec and sendrecv to lock the choice.
sections.eli5: In the example, Alice asks for three things, Bob says no to one of them, and later they tweak the plan by agreeing on new mailboxes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who can change offers or answers in transit could divert media streams (which enables eavesdropping), disable calls, or inject unwanted streams. Someone who only observes the exchange can still inject media into a conversation.

Offer/answer relies on its carrier protocol for security. That protocol MUST provide end-to-end authentication and integrity protection of offers and answers, and SHOULD offer encryption of bodies. Replay is also a problem, for example replaying an old offer that put media on hold, so the carrier MUST give a secure way to sequence offers and answers and reject old ones. The RFC says SIP meets all of these requirements.
sections.eli5: If a sneaky person could change the notes passed between the two kids, they could trick them. So the way the notes are passed has to make sure they are real and not swapped.
